A weekend build combining LangGraph orchestration with OpenMed’s on-device NLP models for automated PHI redaction and clinical entity extraction.
By Kunal Pardhi, Senior AI/ML Engineer
Press enter or click to view image in full size

When building AI solutions for healthcare and life sciences, the biggest roadblock is always the same: Data Privacy.
With strict HIPAA regulations and the catastrophic risks of data egress, you simply cannot send raw patient records to external cloud LLMs. Healthcare enterprises need the intelligence of modern AI, but they need it running entirely on-device, within their own secure networks.
This weekend, I decided to tackle this exact problem by building a proof-of-concept (POC) architecture: A local-first, privacy-by-design clinical agent pipeline.
To do this, I orchestrated a multi-agent workflow that automatically redacts Protected Health Information (PHI) and extracts structured clinical entities (diseases, medications, dosages) — all running 100% locally.
Here is how I built it.

The Tech Stack: Orchestration Meets Local NLP
To build a production-grade enterprise simulation, I combined three key technologies:

• LangGraph (Orchestration): For managing the stateful, multi-agent workflow. LangGraph allows us to define clear, deterministic pathways for data to travel between specialized AI nodes.

• OpenMed (The Heavy Lifter): Created by Maziyar Panahi, OpenMed is a fantastic Apache-2.0 open-source clinical NLP toolkit. Instead of training models from scratch, I leveraged OpenMed’s highly optimized, on-device models for HIPAA-ready de-identification (capable of stripping 55+ PHI types) and clinical Named Entity Recognition (NER).

• FastAPI & Vanilla JS (The UI): To visualize the pipeline in action, I built a lightweight FastAPI backend and a custom, side-by-side document UI that mimics a real hospital “Patient History and Clinical Appendix.”
(Note: A huge shoutout to the OpenMed open-source project. If you are doing local healthcare NLP, it is an absolute goldmine. My goal here was to show how we can wrap these powerful raw models into an automated, agentic architecture).

The Pipeline Architecture
To make this concrete, here is a look at how I structured the LangGraph state and defined the workflow for this POC:
from typing import TypedDict, List, Dict, Any
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END# 1. Define the State Schema
class AgentState(TypedDict):
raw_text: str
sanitized_text: str
extracted_entities: List[Dict[str, Any]]
final_summary: str
error: str
# 2. Initialize the Graph
workflow = StateGraph(AgentState)
# 3. Add nodes and compile graph
workflow.add_node("guardrail", guardrail_node)
workflow.add_node("extractor", extractor_node)
workflow.add_node("synthesis", synthesis_node)
# The critical routing logic: Halt if PHI fails redaction, otherwise proceed
workflow.add_edge(START, "guardrail")
workflow.add_conditional_edges(
"guardrail",
check_privacy_status,
{
"pass": "extractor",
"fail": END
}
)
workflow.add_edge("extractor", "synthesis")
workflow.add_edge("synthesis", END)
The workflow itself is divided into three distinct specialized “agents” (nodes in the graph):
1. The Guardrail Agent (Privacy First)
This is the first line of defense. The moment raw clinical text enters the pipeline, the Guardrail agent intercepts it. Utilizing OpenMed’s de-identification models, it scans for PHI (Names, DOBs, SSNs, Addresses) and redacts them. If a document fails this step, it is halted. No PII is allowed to pass further down the chain.
2. The Extractor Agent (Clinical Intelligence)
Once the text is sanitized, it is passed to the Extractor. This agent is tasked with pure clinical understanding. It identifies diseases, symptoms, medications, and specific dosages from the text, returning structured, high-confidence JSON objects.
3. The Synthesis Agent
Finally, the Synthesis agent compiles the original sanitized text and the structured clinical entities into an audit-ready payload that can be consumed by downstream hospital databases or analytics dashboards.

Bringing it to Life: The Visual UI
Pipelines are great, but seeing is believing. To demonstrate this workflow, I built a UI that visually represents how this would look in a real-world Medical application.
The interface features a two-column view:

• The Left (RAW INPUT): A simulated structured medical document containing highly sensitive mock PII and raw clinical notes.
As you can see in the demo, the moment the pipeline is triggered, the agentic workflow processes the document in real-time. It instantly drops sleek black redaction blocks over all the PII fields (revealing their data labels like [SSN] or [FIRST_NAME] on hover) and cleanly organizes the extracted clinical entities at the bottom. The visual impact is immediate, making the complex backend pipeline tangible and easy to understand for stakeholders.

Why this matters
We are entering the era of Agentic AI. But in highly regulated sectors like life sciences, throwing a massive cloud LLM at a problem isn’t a viable strategy.
By utilizing local-first open-source models like OpenMed and structuring them with robust orchestration frameworks like LangGraph, we can build intelligent, autonomous pipelines that respect patient privacy by design. Data never leaves the local machine, compliance is maintained, and clinical insights are structured perfectly.
If you’re an AI Engineer in healthcare, I highly recommend exploring this stack.
